1.pericope_label: Praise, O ye servants of the LORD
debates: Which psalms make up the Hallel and where it begins
Who the servants summoned to praise are
Whether from the rising of the sun marks time or place
outliers: Calvin reports the psalm may be by Samuel or David on the strength of its borrowings from the song of Hannah, where the others leave the author unnamed
themes: Praise as the debt of those who know God best
A summons that begins at the moment it is heard
Worship bounded by neither age nor country
The name itself as the object of praise

4.pericope_label: High above all nations, yet humbling himself to behold
debates: Whether the word exalted governs both halves of the verse
What the things in heaven that he stoops to behold are
Whether the condescension is measured against earthly greatness or against rival deities
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch decline the parallel usually cited for this verse and construe the sentence from a different one
themes: Incomparability argued from creation and from grace
Greatness that does not make God unapproachable
Providence reaching down through every order of creature

7.pericope_label: He raiseth up the poor out of the dust
debates: Whether the raising is historical, spiritual or eschatological
Who the princes are that the poor man is seated with
Whether the joyful mother is an individual or the nation
outliers: Clarke refers both the raising and the fruitful house to the return from Babylon, where Gill reads them of the church and of spiritual poverty
themes: A borrowed song reused as praise
The rubbish heap as the place of the outcast
Fruitfulness given where it had been despaired of
